scenes.text: The stethoscope was born from embarrassment.
scenes.visual: The hook, under the cover text: close in the ward, the doctor in a grey-blue coat bends over the bed, eyes closed, his ear on the top of a rolled paper tube standing on the young woman's chest; his hand holds it; from the first frame a red bloom beats through her dress and red pulses climb the tube, her chest rises and falls, the light shimmers, his blush deepens.

scenes.text: In 1816, Paris doctor René Laennec faced a young woman with heart trouble.
scenes.visual: A pale hospital ward by day: a tall arched window with light falling in, a wooden bed with a young woman lying under a blanket, and the doctor in a grey-blue coat with a white collar standing large at the foot of the bed, turned toward her. Note 'Necker Hospital, Paris'.

scenes.text: Tapping her chest told him little, and pressing his ear to it was improper.
scenes.visual: Medium shot in the ward: the doctor in a dark coat stands behind the bed, cheeks a little flushed, and taps her chest twice with two fingers (small grey rings fade at once, note 'dull'); then he draws his hand back and 'improper' is written in red above.

scenes.text: Then he recalled a trick children play:
scenes.visual: A courtyard on a soft day, the city's roofs and spire far behind; a long squared timber beam lies on two stone blocks, a child kneeling at each end. Note 'a game'.

scenes.text: scratch one end of a long beam, and listen at the other.
scenes.visual: Close on the beam: at the far (left) end a hand comes in with a pin and scratches the wood; at the near end a child kneels bent over the beam, cheek and ear on the wood; red arcs run through the beam from the pin to the ear. Notes 'a pin' and 'listening' (red).

scenes.text: He rolled paper into a tight tube,
scenes.visual: From above on a writing desk (an inkwell with a quill, the desk's front edge low in frame): a sheet of notepaper with faint handwriting rolls up from its top edge into a tight paper tube; two hands in grey-blue coat sleeves, short forearms coming in from the sides, hold its ends and follow it down.

scenes.text: and set it on her chest. Her heartbeat came through clearer than ever.
scenes.visual: The whole moment wide in the ward (the hook was the close-up): the woman's whole head on the pillow, the doctor bent over her, his ear at the top of the paper tube on her chest, his hand holding it. On 'heartbeat' a red bloom beats under her dress and red pulses run up the tube to his ear. Note 'lub-dub' in red.

scenes.text: Today, his blush hangs around every doctor's neck.
scenes.visual: A specimen plate: the rolled paper tube lies beside a modern stethoscope draped as if round a neck, painting in over a warm bloom. Notes '1816: paper' and 'today'.

scenes.visual: Title card: a small rolled paper tube, 'The paper stethoscope', sub 'Paris, 1816'.

youtube.title: Stethoscope Invention: Why Did a Doctor Roll Up Paper?
youtube.description:
The stethoscope invention began with embarrassment. In 1816, at the Necker Hospital in Paris, Dr René Laennec had to examine a young woman with heart trouble. Tapping her chest told him little, and pressing his ear to a young woman's chest was improper. Then he remembered children scratching one end of a long piece of wood and listening at the other. He rolled a quire of paper into a tube, and her heartbeat came through clearer than ever. He later made it in wood and named it the stethoscope.
